newsitem.title: UK: Good crops seen raising E Europe grain sales to EU.
newsitem.headline: Good crops seen raising E Europe grain sales to EU.

text.p: Improved crops will put some eastern European countries in a better position to take advantage of EU concessions on grain imports, according to the UK's Home Grown Cereals Authority.
But fulfilment of the import quotas, set under EU association agreements, was unlikely to have much effect on the EU's grain market.

The quotas represented only a small proportion of export potential in some countries. For example, the HGCA contrasted a wheat import quota of 22,840 tonnes from Romania for the calendar year 1997 with a total 1997 crop projected at seven million tonnes.
"If crop projections are reached, this should enable some of the associated countries to make sufficient grain available for European traders to bid for," the HGCA said in its Weekly Digest.

Grains production was expected to recover in Romania and Hungary in 1997. But Bulgaria was expected to have another wheat shortfall and floods are expected to have damaged crops in parts of Poland and the Czech Republic, the HGCA said.
Response to the import quotas was good in 1994-95 and also 1995-96 thanks to a generally good Eastern European harvest in those years.

But last year saw adverse weather conditions and therefore a reduction in cereal production. Countries barely able to fulfill their domestic needs were unable to make much available for import by the EU, the HGCA said.

Imports of cereals from these countries were allowed into the EU at reduced tariffs, under two Association Agreements, the first coming into force on 1 February 1994 and involving Hungary, Poland, the Czech and Slovak Republics and the second on 1 February 1995 and involving Bulgaria and Romania.
